**Bottom line:** do this if you want a head start on day 1. Nothing here is marked, recorded or required, and you can
skip any part. The course teaches everything again, live. Reading a block explorer is not in the primer: it is taught on
day 1.

The primer is six short parts: five you click through in your browser, and one short run of slides. Every part opens
from the links below, and nothing needs installing.

## The plan

The times are estimates. They will be checked with test students and changed to match.

| # | Part | What you do | Time |
|---|------|-------------|------|
| 1 | [Hashing](#hashing) | Type text, watch its hash | 15 min |
| 2 | [A tamper-evident ledger](#a-tamper-evident-ledger) | Edit one record, see what breaks | 15 min |
| 3 | [Keys and signatures](#keys-and-signatures) | Try to forge a signed payment; send a copy of one | 15 min |
| 4 | [Distributed systems](#distributed-systems) | Watch two payments spread; see what settles which one counts | 15 min |
| 5 | [Proof-of-work mining](#proof-of-work-mining) | Race a simulated machine 20 times faster | 15 min |
| 6 | [From click to confirmed transaction](#from-click-to-confirmed-transaction) | Nine slides | 30 min |
|   | **Total** | | **about 2 h** |

Take the parts in this order: each uses ideas from the one before.

## Hashing

[Open the hash lab](assets/labs/guess-the-input/){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

A hash function turns any input into a fixed-length fingerprint. SHA-256 is the hash Bitcoin uses; its fingerprint is
64 hexadecimal digits
[@nationalinstituteofstandardsandtechnologyus_securehashstandard_2015; @nakamoto_bitcoinpeertopeerelectronic_2008].
The lab, "Guess the input", asks one question: could a powerful enough computer work a hash backwards to the text that
made it? Predict first, then let your browser hash a sentence of your own, with a counter on the end, until the hash
starts with zeros.

Try this:

1. Predict how many tries it takes to find a hash that starts with three zeros, and how sure you are.
2. Type a sentence and press *Search*. Watch each try's hash: how much does one try resemble the last?
3. Ask for four and five zeros. How much longer does each extra zero take?
4. Read the bars for 19 zeros and 64 zeros. What would "working it backwards" cost?

**You are done when** you can say why nobody can work a hash backwards to its input, only guess.

## A tamper-evident ledger

[Open the lab: Build a ledger in four failures](assets/labs/build-a-ledger-in-four-failures/index.html){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

In a blockchain, each block carries the hash of the block before it
[@nakamoto_bitcoinpeertopeerelectronic_2008]. In four rounds you play the cheat who wants to change an old entry, and
each round's fix arrives because the last design failed. Every hash is real SHA-256.

Try this:

1. Before you start, answer the prediction: can you change entry 2 so the ledger still checks out?
2. Edit entry 2 in round 1, then in round 2 press *Rehash after me*. Do the links hold?
3. Make the fake copies in round 3, then redo the work in round 4. Who wins each time?
4. Read the real block on the explorer view, then answer the twist and write the sentence.

**You are done when** you can explain why editing an old record is visible to everyone holding a copy.

## Keys and signatures

[Open the lab: Forge the payment](assets/labs/forge-the-payment/index.html){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

A digital signature lets anyone check that a message came from the holder of a private key, and that the message was
not changed. A wallet signs a transaction this way [@antonopoulos_masteringethereum_2018].
In the lab, Ana has signed a payment to Ben. You hold a copy of it and a key of your own, and a small ledger accepts
any payment whose signature checks.

Try this:

1. Predict whether you can make the ledger move Ana's money.
2. Change *Pay* to "me" or *Coins* to 3.00, keep Ana's signature copied on, and press *Send to the ledger*. Does her
   signature still fit?
3. Set *Signature* to "my own key signs it" and send again. Whose account does the ledger take the coins from?
4. Press *Send Ana's payment again, byte for byte*, and watch the balances.

**You are done when** you can say why an edited payment fails, why a copy of Ana's payment still runs, and what a
valid signature proves about who sent it.

## Distributed systems

[Open the lab: Who saw it first?](assets/labs/who-saw-it-first/index.html){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

Bitcoin runs on a peer-to-peer network rather than on one central server [@nakamoto_bitcoinpeertopeerelectronic_2008].
In the lab, Alice signs two payments of the same coin and sends them from opposite sides of a twelve-node map.

Try this:

1. Predict which payment ends up on the chain, then press *Send both payments* and watch them spread.
2. Open a western node and an eastern node and compare their waiting lists.
3. Slide the delay and send again: does the split ever go away?
4. Press *A node finds a block* and see which payment survives.

**You are done when** you can say why two nodes can hold different waiting lists, and what makes every node agree on one payment.

## Proof-of-work mining

[Open the mining step](assets/labs/guess-the-input/#mining){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

In proof of work, miners compete to find a number whose hash meets a target; the first to find one adds the next block,
and the network adjusts the difficulty to keep blocks arriving at a steady pace
[@nakamoto_bitcoinpeertopeerelectronic_2008]. This step is the last part of "Guess the input": your laptop races a
simulated machine 20 times faster, hashing real blocks, and you predict how many of 200 blocks your laptop wins. The page
opens at that step.

Try this:

1. Pick how many of 200 blocks your laptop will win, lock it in, then press *Race*.
2. Press *Race* again. Does the count stay the same? Why not?
3. Read the closing note on how the network changes the number of zeros when blocks come too fast.

**You are done when** you can say what a miner is searching for, why more computing power wins more often, and why the
network changes the difficulty.

## From click to confirmed transaction

Last, nine slides from the course's closing lesson, "Blockchain in the Real World". They follow one payment from a
user's click to a recorded transaction, and name each piece in the path: wallet, RPC provider, node, chain
[@antonopoulos_masteringethereum_2018; @ethereumorg_transactions_2025].

Open the first link below, then press the right arrow seven times to reach the eighth slide. The ninth slide sits
further on in the deck, so it has its own link. Stop after it; the rest of the deck is for later in the course. Each
link also opens its own slide.

1. [What does a user actually interact with?](lessons/conclusion/01-AS-blockchain_in_the_real_world.html#/what-does-a-user-actually-interact-with)
2. [Walking a transaction step by step](lessons/conclusion/01-AS-blockchain_in_the_real_world.html#/walking-a-transaction-step-by-step)
3. [Wallets: the control layer](lessons/conclusion/01-AS-blockchain_in_the_real_world.html#/wallets-the-control-layer)
4. [Custody models](lessons/conclusion/01-AS-blockchain_in_the_real_world.html#/custody-models)
5. [What users actually do](lessons/conclusion/01-AS-blockchain_in_the_real_world.html#/what-users-actually-do)
6. [RPC providers: the access layer](lessons/conclusion/01-AS-blockchain_in_the_real_world.html#/rpc-providers-the-access-layer)
7. [Nodes and validators](lessons/conclusion/01-AS-blockchain_in_the_real_world.html#/nodes-and-validators)
8. [The full blockchain system](lessons/conclusion/01-AS-blockchain_in_the_real_world.html#/the-full-blockchain-system)
9. [Bridges: linking separate chains](lessons/conclusion/01-AS-blockchain_in_the_real_world.html#/bridges-linking-separate-chains)

The ninth slide is only the basics: blockchains do not share assets with each other, so a bridge locks a token on one
chain and issues a linked copy on another, which adds trust and security risk [@l31_ethereumorg_blockchainbridges_2026].

**You are done when** you can say, in your own words, what happens between pressing *send* and the transaction being
recorded.

## What happens next

Day 1 starts from these ideas and goes further: blocks and chains, keys on secp256k1, addresses, and reading a real
transaction in an explorer. Bring any question the primer raised.
